items.title: Somalia’s 40% Customs Revenue Shock Raises Questions Over Government Finances
items.description: MOGADISHU (WDN) — Somalia’s federal government is facing mounting fiscal pressure after President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud disclosed that customs-based domestic revenue has fallen by an estimated 40 percent , underscoring the vulnerability of the country’s finances to disruptions in regional maritime trade. The president attributed the decline to disruptions around the Strait of Hormuz, a critical global shipping corridor, which have affected trade and increased the cost of imported goods. He warned that Somalia’s heavy dependence on imports from the Middle East has left the country particularly exposed to instability along major maritime trade routes. The disclosure is significant because customs duties collected at ports and other entry points represent an important source of domestic government revenue. A sharp reduction in customs receipts can directly constrain the government’s ability to finance public services, economic programmes and other recurrent expenditures. The president did not specify the period covered by the 40 percent estimate or provide detailed figures comparing customs collections before and after the decline. Earlier government data, however, indicated that the volume of goods entering Somalia had also fallen by nearly 40 percent during the maritime disruption, although the two figures measure different things. A Fiscal Shock Beyond the Ports The consequences extend beyond government accounts. Somalia is heavily dependent on imported food, fuel, medicines and other essential commodities. Disruptions to shipping routes can therefore affect both the volume and cost of goods entering the country. President Hassan Sheikh said the maritime crisis had contributed to higher food and fuel prices, inflation, transport costs and insurance premiums. Earlier government assessments also reported significant increases in food and healthcare costs amid the disruption. For an economy already struggling with limited domestic revenue, drought and humanitarian pressures, the combination of falling customs receipts and rising import costs presents a particularly difficult fiscal challenge. The government is effectively facing pressure from both directions: less revenue coming into the treasury while the cost of goods and services continues to rise. Salary Delays Add to the Concern Against this backdrop, reports have emerged that some members of the National Intelligence and Security Agency (NISA) have not received their salaries on their normal payment date this month. According to reports, some NISA personnel who did receive their salaries were allegedly paid $200 instead of the reported $280, representing an $80 reduction. There are also reports that members of the Somali Custodial Corps have gone without salaries for more than a year. However, these claims have not been independently confirmed, and senior officials responsible for NISA and the custodial service have not publicly addressed the reports. It would therefore be premature to directly attribute the alleged salary problems to the 40 percent decline in customs revenue. Nevertheless, the reports have raised questions about the broader financial pressures facing the federal government. If confirmed, prolonged salary delays affecting security and corrections personnel would carry consequences beyond household finances. Regular and predictable payment of security-sector salaries is closely linked to morale, institutional stability and the government’s ability to maintain essential state functions. Somalia’s Exposure to Regional Disruption The deeper problem highlighted by the customs-revenue decline is Somalia’s vulnerability to external economic shocks. The country imports a substantial share of the goods it consumes, leaving government revenue and household purchasing power sensitive to developments far beyond Somalia’s borders. The disruption of shipping through strategic waterways such as Hormuz and the Bab el-Mandeb can alter shipping routes, increase insurance premiums and transportation costs, delay cargo and ultimately affect both customs collections and consumer prices. Recent reporting has shown Somali traders and shipping interests exploring alternative routes as insecurity around regional maritime corridors disrupts established supply chains. For Somalia, this means that maritime security is not simply an international geopolitical issue. It has a direct connection to the national budget, the cost of living and the government’s capacity to pay for essential services. The 40 percent customs-revenue decline should therefore be viewed as more than a temporary fall in government income. It exposes a structural weakness: Somalia remains heavily dependent on trade-based taxation while its domestic revenue base is still relatively narrow. That vulnerability becomes particularly serious when the government is simultaneously expected to finance security operations, public-sector salaries, social services, infrastructure, economic reforms and development programmes. President Hassan Sheikh has said his government is continuing efforts to strengthen domestic revenue collection, public financial management and budget transparency despite external economic pressures. He also told the UN General Assembly that Somalia’s economy is expected to record real growth of 3.1 percent this year. But the customs shock raises a more fundamental question: How resilient is Somalia’s fiscal system when an international shipping crisis thousands of kilometers away can remove such a large portion of customs-based domestic revenue? That question deserves urgent attention. From Maritime Crisis to National Budget The lesson from the current disruption is clear. Somalia cannot fully insulate itself from regional instability, but it can reduce the impact by broadening its domestic revenue base, improving customs administration, diversifying the economy and strengthening mechanisms that protect essential government spending during external shocks. The reported salary difficulties, if independently confirmed, would provide another warning that fiscal pressures can quickly move from government balance sheets into the daily functioning of state institutions. For a country seeking to strengthen its institutions and reduce dependence on external assistance, the 40 percent customs-revenue decline is therefore more than an economic statistic. It is a warning about the fragility of the revenue system—and a reminder that Somalia’s economic stability can be profoundly affected by events taking place far beyond its shores. items.title: Hassan Sheikh’s Israel-Türkiye Contradiction Raises Questions Over Somalia’s Foreign Policy
items.description: President Rejects Any Comparison Between Israel and Türkiye — Yet Leaves the Door Open to Future Relations with Israel MOGADISHU (WDN) — President Hassan Sheikh Mohamud’s latest interview with Al Jazeera has exposed a striking tension in Somalia’s foreign-policy messaging: while he presents Türkiye as fundamentally different from Israel and rejects any suggestion that the two countries could be treated alike, he also acknowledges that Somalia could one day establish relations with Israel. The apparent contradiction is significant because Hassan Sheikh has adopted an increasingly uncompromising position toward Israel since Israel recognized Somaliland.In his latest Al Jazeera interview, the president said Somalia would not accept an Israeli presence “under any circumstances” and accused Israel of seeking a military foothold in Berbera. He described Israel as a destabilizing force and said Somalia would resist attempts to draw the country into wider Middle Eastern conflicts. Yet the president’s position appears more nuanced when he discusses the possibility of diplomatic relations. He has indicated that Israel could, under different circumstances, become a country with which Somalia maintains relations in the future, while insisting that Israel could never replace Türkiye as Somalia’s principal strategic partner. That raises a straightforward question: If relations with Israel are fundamentally unacceptable, under what circumstances could they become possible? Türkiye Is Different — But Why? Hassan Sheikh’s distinction between Türkiye and Israel is clear. Türkiye is a Muslim-majority country with longstanding political, economic and security ties to Somalia. Ankara has become one of Mogadishu’s most important international partners, particularly in defense, development and diplomatic affairs. Israel, by contrast, recognized Somaliland in December 2025, becoming the first country to do so. Somalia regards Somaliland as part of its sovereign territory and has strongly condemned Israel’s decision. The president therefore has a clear political basis for treating the two relationships differently. But the difficulty emerges when the argument moves from “Israel is not Türkiye” to “Israel could never have the same relationship with Somalia” and then to “perhaps Somalia could have relations with Israel in the future.” Those positions can coexist, but only if the conditions for such a future relationship are clearly explained. At present, they remain largely undefined. The President’s message has changed with circumstances. The evolution of Hassan Sheikh’s statements is also important. After Israel recognized Somaliland, he described the decision as a dangerous strategic move and suggested that Israeli objectives extended beyond diplomatic recognition. He also raised concerns about possible Israeli military and population-transfer plans involving Somaliland. Those claims were presented by the president as intelligence-based concerns, but some of the specific allegations have not been independently established. In his latest interview, Hassan Sheikh went further, saying Israel planned to establish a naval base in Berbera and use the city’s airport. Al Jazeera reported those statements as claims made by the president; Israel’s alleged plans were not independently established in the report. At the same time, the president leaves open the theoretical possibility of future relations. That creates a foreign-policy question that deserves a clearer answer: What would have to change before Israel moves from being described as a threat to becoming a possible diplomatic partner? Would Israel have to reverse its recognition of Somaliland? Would it have to abandon any military ambitions in Berbera? Would Somalia require a change in Israeli policy toward Somaliland before diplomatic relations could even be considered? The president has not publicly provided a detailed framework for such a transition. Somaliland Is the Central Fault Line The contradiction becomes even more important because Somaliland sits at the center of the dispute. Israel’s recognition of Somaliland fundamentally changed the diplomatic environment surrounding the territory. News wires  reported earlier this year that Somaliland expected expanded economic relations with Israel and was seeking investment and technology cooperation, although at that stage no formal economic agreement had been concluded and Somaliland’s president said military bases had not been discussed. For Mogadishu, however, the issue is not simply bilateral relations between Israel and Somaliland. It is a question of Somalia’s territorial integrity. That explains why Hassan Sheikh has responded so strongly to Israel’s involvement. But it also means that any future discussion of Somali-Israeli relations would almost certainly have to address the Somaliland question first. The Bigger Question: is foreign policy being driven by principles or circumstances?  This is where the president’s statements raise a broader issue. Somalia’s foreign policy cannot simply be defined by whether a country is Muslim, non-Muslim, friendly or hostile. States normally assess foreign relationships according to national interests, sovereignty, security, economic benefits and diplomatic objectives. Türkiye’s partnership with Somalia is an example of this pragmatic approach. Somalia has built deep security and economic relations with Türkiye because successive governments have viewed Ankara as an important strategic partner. The same principle could theoretically apply to any other country. But if Somalia is prepared to consider relations with Israel in the future, the government should explain what national-interest conditions would make such a relationship acceptable. Without that explanation, the public is left with two apparently competing messages: Israel is unacceptable — but relations with Israel may one day be possible. A government can reject a country’s current policies while leaving open the possibility of future diplomatic relations if those policies change. But that distinction needs to be made clearly. Somalia’s president has been unequivocal in condemning Israel’s recognition of Somaliland and in warning against Israeli military involvement in the Horn of Africa. If his government nevertheless believes that relations with Israel could eventually be established, then the conditions for such a transformation should be stated openly. Otherwise, the issue risks becoming less about foreign policy and more about political messaging. And that is the real inconsistency exposed by the interview. The question is not whether Türkiye and Israel are the same. They clearly are not. The question is whether Somalia’s foreign policy has a consistent principle for deciding when a country is a strategic partner, when it is a threat, and when it can become a partner in the future. For Hassan Sheikh, that distinction now requires a clearer explanation. Because in foreign policy, leaving the door open while publicly declaring the relationship unacceptable may be politically convenient—but it also invites questions about what is really behind the door. items.title: Ciidamada Eritrea oo gudaha u galay Itoobiya iyo dagaal laga…
items.description: Addis Ababa (Caasimada Online) – Xiisadda u dhexeysa Itoobiya iyo Eritrea ayaa gaartay heer cusub oo halis ah, kadib markii ciidamada Eritrea lagu soo warramay inay gudaha u galeen waqooyiga Itoobiya, halka xukuumadda Addis Ababa ay Asmara ku eedeysay duullaan cusub oo ay dalbatay in ciidamadaasi dib loo saaro. Dhaqdhaqaaqyada cusub ayaa imaanaya xilli ciidamada dowladda Itoobiya iyo xoogag Tigray ah oo taageersan ay ku sii jeedaan waqooyiga gobolka Tigray, una sii dhowaanayaan xadka Eritrea. Warbaahinta Bloomberg ayaa Arbacadii werisay in Itoobiya ay Eritrea ku eedeysay inay ciidamo dheeraad ah soo gelisay dhulkeeda, isla markaana ay dalbatay inay si degdeg ah uga baxaan. Laba qof oo ku nool magaalada Adigrat, oo ku dhow xadka Eritrea, ayaa Reuters u sheegay inay Arbacadii arkeen laba gaari oo siday tobannaan askari oo Eritrean ah oo dhex maraya magaalada. Dadka deegaanka ayaa sheegay inay ciidamada ku garteen direyskooda gaarka ah, inkastoo Reuters ay sheegtay in aysan si madax-bannaan u xaqiijin karin xogtaas. Wakaaladda AFP ayaa sidoo kale sheegtay in ciidamo Eritrean ah lagu arkay agagaarka Adigrat maalmihii lasoo dhaafay, iyadoo qaar ka mid ah ciidamadaas lagu warramay inay dhanka koonfureed ugu sii jeedeen magaalada Mekelle. Adigrat waxay qiyaastii 40 kiiloomitir u jirtaa Eritrea, halka Mekelle ay dhanka koonfureed uga jirto in ka badan 100 kiiloomitir. Ciidamada oo isu soo dhowaanaya Dhaqdhaqaaqyada Eritrea lagu eedeeyay ayaa kusoo aadaya xilli ciidamada federaalka Itoobiya iyo xoogag Tigray ah oo garab siinaya ay waqooyi u sii dhaqaaqayaan kadib markii ay maalmo kahor galeen Mekelle. TPLF ayaa magaalada isaga baxday iyada oo aan dagaal weyn ka dhicin, kadib markii ciidamada dowladda ay dib ula wareegeen dhulal badan oo ay lumiyeen tan iyo markii dagaallada cusub ay billowdeen. Taliye ka tirsan xoogagga Tigray Peace Force, oo dhinaca dowladda Itoobiya dagaalka uga jira, ayaa AFP u sheegay in ciidamadiisu gaareen magaalada Wukro oo qiyaastii 50 kiiloomitir waqooyi kaga beegan Mekelle, kuna taalla waddada weyn ee aadda Eritrea. Arrintan ayaa la micno ah in ciidamada taageersan dowladda Itoobiya iyo kuwa Eritrea ee lagu soo warramayo inay gudaha Tigray joogaan ay sii isu soo dhowaanayaan. Eritrea ayaa dhinaceeda beenisay inay ciidamadeedu gudaha u galeen Adigrat. Wasiirka warfaafinta Eritrea Yemane Gebremeskel ayaa Reuters u sheegay in wararkaasi qeyb ka yihiin isku day Itoobiya ay ku dooneyso inay marmarsiinyo ugu sameysato waxa uu ku tilmaamay “dagaal gardarro ah” oo ka dhan ah Eritrea. Itoobiya ayaa horay Eritrea ugu eedeysay inay taageerto isbahaysi hubeysan oo ay hormuud ka tahay TPLF, kaas oo tan iyo dabayaaqadii bishii September dagaallo kula jiray ciidamada federaalka. Eritrea ayaa marar badan beenisay eedeymahaas. Xiriirka oo gebi ahaan burburay Xiisadda hadda taagan waxay daba socotaa bilo ay sii xumaanayeen xiriirka Addis Ababa iyo Asmara. Itoobiya ayaa bishii February Eritrea ku eedeysay inay ciidamo dheeraad ah soo gelisay dhulkeeda, iyadoo tallaabadaas ku tilmaantay “gardarro cad”. Eritrea ayaa eedeyntaasi diiday. Xiriirka labada dal ayaa sii xumaaday kadib markii dagaallada cusub ay ka qarxeen waqooyiga Itoobiya. 1-dii October, Itoobiya waxay xirtay safaaraddeedii Asmara, waxayna dalka ka cayrisay 10 diblomaasi oo Eritrean ah, iyadoo ku eedeysay Eritrea falal ay sheegtay inay halis ku yihiin amniga qaranka Itoobiya. Eritrea ayaa jawaab ahaan xiriirka diblomaasiyadeed u jartay Itoobiya, waxayna xirtay safaaraddeedii Addis Ababa. Midowga Afrika ayaa kadib labada dhinac iyo dalalka kale ee gobolka ugu baaqay inay muujiyaan xakameyn, kana fogaadaan tallaabo kasta oo sii hurin karta xaaladda Geeska Afrika. Xulafo hore oo isu beddelay cadow Xiisadda cusub waxay astaan u tahay sida weyn ee uu isu beddelay xiriirka Ra’iisul Wasaaraha Itoobiya Abiy Ahmed iyo Madaxweynaha Eritrea Isaias Afwerki. Labada dowladood waxay hal dhinac ka wada dagaallameen dagaalkii Tigray ee 2020 ilaa 2022, markaas oo ciidamada Eritrea ay garab siinayeen kuwa federaalka Itoobiya ee la dagaallamayay TPLF. Hase yeeshee Eritrea qeyb kama ahayn heshiiskii Pretoria ee November 2022 lagu soo afjaray dagaalkaas, waxaana wixii markaas ka dambeeyay si tartiib ah u xumaaday xiriirka Addis Ababa iyo Asmara. Khilaafka waxaa sii huriyay ololaha Itoobiya ay ku dooneyso marin ay ku gaarto Badda Cas. Itoobiya, oo aan lahayn bad tan iyo markii Eritrea ay madax-bannaanida qaadatay 1993, ayaa marar badan sheegtay in helitaanka marin badeed la isku halleyn karo uu muhiim u yahay dhaqaalaheeda iyo amnigeeda qaranka. Hadalkaas ayaa walaac weyn ka abuuray Eritrea, gaar ahaan marka madaxda Itoobiya ay soo hadal qaadaan dekedda istiraatiijiga ah ee Assab. Addis Ababa waxay ku adkeysaneysaa inay marin badeed ku raadineyso wada-hadal iyo heshiis, halka Asmara ay Itoobiya ku eedeysay inay arrinta badda u adeegsaneyso marmarsiinyo ay cadaadis ugu saarto Eritrea. Labada dal ayaa horey u galay dagaal xuduudeed dhiig badan ku daatay intii u dhaxeysay 1998 iyo 2000, kaas oo ay ku dhinteen tobannaan kun oo qof. Xiriirkooda ayaa dib loo soo celiyay 2018 kadib heshiis ay gaareen Abiy Ahmed iyo Isaias Afwerki, balse sideed sano kadib labada dal waxay mar kale jareen xiriirka diblomaasiyadeed, iyadoo ciidamadooda lagu soo warramayo inay si aan hore loo arag ugu sii dhawaanayaan waqooyiga Itoobiya. items.title: Turkey’s Somalia Gamble: How Far Can Ankara Go Before Its Partnership Becomes a Political Liability?
items.description: By Mohamed A Yasin President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan has announced that Türkiye has begun building a spaceport in Somalia, describing the project as a historic partnership that will strengthen Ankara’s independent access to space and contribute to Africa’s emerging space sector. The announcement is extraordinary in itself. But in Somalia, it raises a question far beyond rockets and satellites: How deeply has Türkiye invested itself in Somalia’s political future—and what happens to that relationship when the political leadership in Mogadishu changes? Erdoğan made the announcement at the opening of the 77th International Astronautical Congress in Antalya, saying Somalia’s geographical position gives Türkiye strategic advantages for space launches. Turkish officials have previously described the planned facility as a way for Ankara to secure independent access to orbital launch capability. The spaceport is only the latest expression of an extraordinary expansion of Turkish influence in Somalia. Türkiye has moved from humanitarian assistance and development cooperation into defence, training, infrastructure, energy, diplomacy and strategic security cooperation. That expansion once made Ankara one of the most popular foreign partners among many ordinary Somalis. But the political environment is changing. And so is the public perception of Türkiye. From Humanitarian Partner to Strategic Power Türkiye’s relationship with Somalia was initially built on an image very different from that of a conventional foreign military power. Erdoğan’s highly publicised visit to Mogadishu in 2011, at the height of Somalia’s famine, generated enormous goodwill. Türkiye subsequently invested heavily in hospitals, schools, roads, infrastructure and humanitarian programmes. It also established one of its most important overseas military training facilities in Mogadishu, while Turkish companies became increasingly involved in Somalia’s economy. The relationship deepened further through defence agreements and broader strategic cooperation. By 2026, the partnership had become far more than development assistance. Türkiye had become a major security partner of the Federal Government. That transformation has created enormous strategic influence—but it has also created political risks. Somalia’s current crisis is not simply an insurgency against Al-Shabaab. It is also a political confrontation over constitutional authority, elections, federalism and the distribution of power between Mogadishu and the federal member states. EUAA reporting describes Somalia’s political environment in 2026 as deeply divided, with Puntland and Jubaland opposing Hassan Sheikh’s government and the Federal Government deploying forces to regain control of Baidoa after relations with former South West State President Abdiaziz Hassan Mohamed Laftagareen collapsed. That is where Türkiye’s growing security role becomes politically sensitive. Military assistance intended to strengthen Somalia’s national security institutions becomes far more controversial when those institutions are deployed in conflicts involving Somali political factions. The distinction is crucial. Helping Somalia fight Al-Shabaab is one thing. Becoming associated with one side of Somalia’s internal political confrontation is another. The F-16 and Drone Question Opposition figures and supporters of former President Hassan Sheikh’s political opponents have alleged that Turkish-supplied or Turkish-linked military capabilities, including advanced drones and F-16 aircraft, have been used in operations against opposition forces. Those allegations have generated considerable anger and concern among communities affected by the fighting. But they require careful verification. There is currently clear evidence of Turkish defence cooperation with Somalia, and there is independent evidence that the Federal Government has increasingly used air and drone capabilities during the country’s security operations. EUAA, citing ACLED data, recorded a sharp increase in air and drone strikes in Somalia, reaching 433 incidents between April 2025 and March 2026. There is also clear evidence that Baidoa has become a battlefield between federal forces and forces aligned with Laftagareen. Reuters reported that federal troops and opposition forces fought inside Baidoa on August 17, with residents reporting deaths including civilians. The city also contains large numbers of displaced people already suffering from severe humanitarian conditions. What remains essential is establishing which aircraft conducted particular strikes, who authorized them and whether foreign-supplied military equipment was used in political rather than counterterrorism operations. Those questions cannot be answered by political claims alone. But Perception Can Be as Powerful as Proof. There is another problem for Türkiye. Even where allegations remain unproven, perception matters. If ordinary Somalis begin to associate Turkish military assistance not with the defence of the Somali state but with the suppression of political opposition, Ankara risks losing the public goodwill accumulated over more than a decade. That would represent a dramatic reversal. The Turkish flag once carried associations with humanitarian assistance, hospitals, development and solidarity. It now increasingly appears alongside questions about military power and political influence. For Ankara, this is a dangerous transformation. Foreign governments can negotiate agreements with presidents. They cannot easily negotiate with public opinion. What Happens After Hassan Sheikh? This may ultimately be the most important question in the entire relationship. Hassan Sheikh Mohamud will not remain president forever. Every Somali government eventually changes. Every political alliance eventually shifts. Every foreign partnership must therefore survive political transition if it is genuinely a partnership with the Somali state rather than a relationship with one administration. The deeper Türkiye becomes identified with the political and security choices of the current Federal Government, the more vulnerable its long-term position becomes if a future government takes a different view of Ankara. That is not an argument against Turkish involvement in Somalia. It is an argument for institutional neutrality. A foreign power seeking a permanent relationship with Somalia has an interest in maintaining relations not only with the government in power, but also with opposition leaders, federal member states, civil society and the Somali public. Otherwise, today’s strategic partner can become tomorrow’s political target. The Spaceport Makes the Question Even Bigger The planned spaceport dramatically expands the horizon of the relationship. Türkiye is not merely training Somali soldiers. It is developing infrastructure that Erdoğan says will contribute to Türkiye’s independent access to space. Turkish officials have explicitly described Somalia’s equatorial geography as strategically advantageous for launch operations. That means Ankara’s long-term interests in Somalia could extend well beyond the political lifespan of any current Somali administration. Ports, Energy, Defence, Infrastructure, Aerospace, Security, Diplomacy. The relationship is becoming extraordinarily broad. And the broader the relationship becomes, the more important it is that it be seen as a relationship with Somalia, rather than with one political camp. Civilian Casualties Change the Equation For ordinary Somalis, strategic partnerships are ultimately judged by what they mean for everyday life. A spaceport may represent technological ambition. A military aircraft may represent national defense. A drone may represent counterterrorism. But for a civilian caught beneath a strike, none of those distinctions matter if a home is destroyed or a family member is killed. The reported civilian casualties surrounding political and military confrontations in Baidoa therefore deserve independent investigation, regardless of which side is responsible. Reuters reported civilian deaths during the August fighting, while Baidoa remains one of Somalia’s major displacement and humanitarian centres. If foreign-supported military capabilities are involved in operations that cause civilian harm, the political consequences can extend far beyond the battlefield. Somalia also has the right to seek Turkish investment, training, technology and security assistance. But a sustainable partnership requires something more than agreements between governments. It requires public confidence. Türkiye therefore faces a strategic choice. It can become identified primarily with the political administration currently controlling Villa Somalia. Or it can position itself as a long-term partner of the Somali state—one capable of maintaining constructive relations regardless of who occupies the presidency. The second approach would be considerably safer for Ankara. A Strategic Partnership Cannot Depend on One President The central paradox of Türkiye’s growing presence in Somalia is now becoming clear. The more Ankara invests in Somalia, the more it needs Somalia’s political stability. But the more its military and strategic involvement becomes associated with one side of Somalia’s political conflict, the greater the risk that its long-term interests will become entangled with the fate of that political side. That is the danger. Hassan Sheikh will eventually leave office. The Federal Government will change. Political alliances will change. Federal-state relations will change. Türkiye’s relationship with Somalia was once built largely on humanitarian solidarity and development. Today it is becoming a relationship of military power, strategic infrastructure and geopolitical ambition. The question facing Ankara is therefore no longer whether it can expand its influence in Somalia. Because if Türkiye becomes seen by ordinary Somalis as a party to the political conflict rather than a partner of Somalia itself, the consequences may last long after the government that invited Ankara into the centre of Somali affairs has gone. The spaceport may be designed to reach far into the future. Türkiye’s political strategy in Somalia should be designed the same way. The announcement is extraordinary in itself. But in Somalia, it raises a question far beyond rockets and satellites: How deeply has Türkiye invested itself in Somalia’s political future—and what happens to that relationship when the political leadership in Mogadishu changes? Erdoğan made the announcement at the opening of the 77th International Astronautical Congress in Antalya, saying Somalia’s geographical position gives Türkiye strategic advantages for space launches. Turkish officials have previously described the planned facility as a way for Ankara to secure independent access to orbital launch capability. The spaceport is only the latest expression of an extraordinary expansion of Turkish influence in Somalia. Türkiye has moved from humanitarian assistance and development cooperation into defence, training, infrastructure, energy, diplomacy and strategic security cooperation. That expansion once made Ankara one of the most popular foreign partners among many ordinary Somalis. But the political environment is changing. And so is the public perception of Türkiye. From Humanitarian Partner to Strategic Power Türkiye’s relationship with Somalia was initially built on an image very different from that of a conventional foreign military power. Erdoğan’s highly publicised visit to Mogadishu in 2011, at the height of Somalia’s famine, generated enormous goodwill. Türkiye subsequently invested heavily in hospitals, schools, roads, infrastructure and humanitarian programmes. It also established one of its most important overseas military training facilities in Mogadishu, while Turkish companies became increasingly involved in Somalia’s economy. The relationship deepened further through defence agreements and broader strategic cooperation. By 2026, the partnership had become far more than development assistance. Türkiye had become a major security partner of the Federal Government. That transformation has created enormous strategic influence—but it has also created political risks. Military assistance intended to strengthen Somalia’s national security institutions becomes far more controversial when those institutions are deployed in conflicts involving Somali political factions. EUAA, citing ACLED data, recorded a sharp increase in air and drone strikes in Somalia, reaching 433 incidents between April 2025 and March 2026. There is also clear evidence that Baidoa has become a battlefield between federal forces and forces aligned with Laftagareen. The city also contains large numbers of displaced people already suffering from severe humanitarian conditions. items.title: Miisaanka Istaratijiga ah ee Somaliland oo sii Kordhaya iyo Washington oo Indhaha ku-haysa”
items.description: Warbaahinta Kenya Insights ayaa sheegtay in miisaanka istaraatiijiga ah ee Jamhuuriyadda Somaliland uu si weyn u sii xoogaysanayo, xilli Washington ay sii kordhinayso danaynteeda ku aaddan muhiimadda juqraafiyeed ee Somaliland, gaar ahaan Dekedda Berbera iyo goobta ay kaga taallo marin-biyoodka muhiimka ah ee Gacanka Cadmeed. Warbixintu waxay xustay in isbeddellada cusub ee ka socda Badda Cas iyo Gacanka Cadmeed ay mar kale iftiimiyeen muhiimadda juqraafiyadeed ee Somaliland, iyadoo si gaar ah loo tilmaamay Berbera oo ku dhow marin-biyoodka Bab el-Mandeb, oo ah marin muhiim u ah isku socodka ganacsiga caalamiga ah ee u dhexeeya Badweynta Hindiya, Badda Cas iyo Kanaalka Suweys. Kenya Insights ayaa falanqaysay sida siyaasadda Washington ee Geeska Afrika ay u yeelanayso dhinacyo cusub, iyadoo Somaliland ay si isa soo taraysa ugu dhex muuqanayso xisaabaha istaraatiijiga ah e dawladda Maraykanka iyo guud ahaan xiisaha caalamiga ah ee la xidhiidha doodaha amniga Badda Cas, ganacsiga caalamiga ah iyo iskaashiga istaraatiijiga ah. Warbixintu waxay tilmaamaysaa in booqashadii Madaxweynaha Somaliland Dr. Cabdiraxmaan Maxamed Cabdillaahi (Cirro) ku tagay Washington ay soo bandhigay fursadaha istaraatiijiga ah iyo kuwa dhaqaale ee Somaliland leedahay. Iyadoo kulamadii ka dhacay Washington iyo New York diiradda lagu saaray arrimo badan oo ay ka mid ahaayeen muhiimadda Dekedda Berbera iyo Garoonka Caalamiga ah ee Berbera, khayraadka macdanta, fursadaha iskaashi ee dhinaca amniga iyo goobta juqraafiyeed ee Somaliland kaga taallo Gacanka Cadmeed. Warbixinru waxay tilmaantay in arrintani ay muujinayso in xidhiidhka diblumaasiyadeed ee Somaliland iyo Maraykanku aanay ku koobnayn oo keliya arrinta aqoonsiga, balse ay sii ballaadhanayso, isla markaana ay leedahay dhinacyo kale oo muhiim ah oo ay ka mid yihiin dano dhaqaale, amni iyo istaraatiijiyadeed. Sidoo kale waxa laugu xusay warbixinta muhiimadda magaalo xeebeeda Berbera, taas oo warbixintu ku tilmaanay qodobada ugu muhiimsan ee Somaliland ka dhigaya meel ay si gaar ah u danaynqyqan quwadaha caalamka. Kenya Insights waxay xustay in Dekedda Dekeda Berbera ay ku taallao xeebta Gacanka Cadmeed, iyadoo u dhow Bab el-Mandeb, oo ka mid ah marin-biyoodka ugu muhiimsan ee isku xidha Badda Cas iyo Badweynta Hindiya. Sida ay sheegtay warbixintu, muhiimadda Berbera kuma koobna arrimaha Somaliland oo keliya, balse waxay si dhow ula xidhiidhaa amniga iyo ganacsiga marinnada badda ee caalamiga ah. Warbixintu waxay sidoo kale xustay saamaynta go’aankii ay Israel ku aqoonsatau Somaliland 26-kii December 2025. Iyada oo tilmaantay in tallaabadaasi ay Somaliland u abuurtay marxalad cusub oo diblomaasiyadeed iyo fursado badan oo istaraatiiji ah. Sidoo kale waxay xustay, in Washington ay muujinayso marxalad cusub oo la xidhiidha xiisaha iyo danaynta Somaliland in kasta oo Maraykanku aanu weli si rasmi ah u aqoonsan. Waxa kale oo ay sheegtay in Washington ay diiradda ssarayso dano amni, dhaqaale iyo istaraatiijiyadeed. Maadaama ay, Somaliland ku taallo goob istaraatiiji ah oo u dhow mid ka mid ah marinnada badda ee ugu muhiimsan dunida. Warbixinta ayaa tilmaantay in isku dhaca danahan istaraatiiga ah ee dawladda Maraykanka iyo humiimadda gobolka Geeska Afrika ay Somaliland ka dhigeen meel si gaar ah u soo jiidanaysa indhaha siyaasiyiinta, diblumaasiyionta iyo hay’adaha amniga ee Washington. Warbixinta Kenya Insights waxay iftiiminaysaa sida Somaliland ay si isa soo taraysa ugu dhex muuqanayso xisaabta istaraatiijiga ah ee Badda Cas iyo Gacanka Cadmeed. Marka la eego xogta ay soo bandhigtay Kenya Insights, Somaliland waxay leedahay dhowr arrimood oo kor u qaadaya miisaankeeda istaraatiijiga ah: goob juqraafiyeed muhiim ah, Dekedda Berbera, Garoonka Caalamiga ah ee Berbera iyo u-dhowaanshaha marinnada Badda Cas.

items.title: Shariif oo sheegay in dowladdu weerarayso mucaaradka kadib safarkii Imaaraadka
items.description: Muqdisho (Caasimada Online) – Madaxweynihii hore ee Soomaaliya, Shariif Sheekh Axmed oo kasoo laabtay safar uu ku tegay dalka Imaaraadka Carabta ayaa sheegay in dowladda uu hoggaamiyo Madaxweyne Xasan Sheekh ay uga qiil dhiganayso safarkiisa si ay u weerarto hoggaanka mucaaradka. “Imaaraadka waan degenahay, saddex maalin ayaa soo joogay, caruurteyda degan, arrimo qoys ayaa u tegay. Weligay ayaa deganaa oo tegi jiray. Ma noqon karto asbaab lagu baneysan karo dhiigga dadka mucaaradka ah ee u taagan in dastuurka la ixtiraamo oo doorashadana laga heshiiyo,” ayuu yiri Shariif. Waxa uu intaas kusii daray “Ma jirto sabab farta loogu fiiqi karo (mucaaradka). Waxaa la fahamsan yahay in cidda dhibaatada wada inay tahay cidda kale (dowladda).” Shariifka ayaa hoggaanka dowladda ku eedeeyay in si qaldan u adeegsanayo hay’adihii kala duwanaa ee dowladda iyo ciidamadii qaranka oo dadka lagu dhibaateynayo, sida uu hadalka u dhigay. “Hadii dastuurka laga tago wadda-hadaladana la iska diido, jihada la aadayo waa la yaqaan, suuragalna ma ahan in la yiraahdo mucaarad ayaa la wareerayaa,” ayuu yiri. Waxa uu intaas kusii daray “Dalkii wuxuu kusoo koobnay hal gacan, mas’uuliyadaas haddii wax ka dhacaan dalka ama dagaal ka dhaco waxay taabaneysa hoggaanka dowladda iyo xukuumadda ka shaqeynaysa ee hantidii qaranka ku bixinaysa in dhiig la daadsho.” Shariif ayaa ka digay in tegitaanka mucaaradka ee Imaaraadka loogu qiil sameysto weerar lagu qaado, xilli dhawaan Wasiirka Gaashaandhigga Soomaaliya uu soccaalka mucaaradka ee Abu Dhabi la xiriiriyay qorshe abaabul dagaal oo mucaaradka ka bilaabayo Muqdisho. Fiqi ayaa ku eedeeyay siyaasiyiinta mucaaradka ah inay Abu Dhabi kula kulmeen dhinacyo xiriir la leh RSF, isagoo sheegay in kulamadaasi ay la xiriiraan qorshayaal looga soo horjeedo dowladnimada Soomaaliya. Wasiirka ayaa sidoo kale ku eedeeyay mucaaradka in ay la soo noqon doonaan shirqoollo ka dhan ah dowladnimada iyo nabadda, ayna isku dayi doonaan inay maleeshiyaad uruuris iyo hoggaamiye-kooxeednimo bilaabaan, sida uu hadalka u dhigay. Dowladda Soomaaliya ayuu sheegay inay waajib ku tahay inay si adag uga hortagto cid walba oo halis gelinaysa nabadda iyo dowladnimada, qaranimada iyo madax-bannaanida dalka. “Khaa’inul-wadan kastaana abaalkiisa la marsiin doono,” ayuu Fiqi ku yiri qoraal uu dhawaan soo saaray. Si kastaba, arrimahan ayaa imanaya xilli xiisadda siyaasadeed ee dalka ay mareyso meel xasaasi ah, isla markaana ay mucaaradka iyo dowladda isku mari la’yihiin doorashooyinka iyo wax ka beddelka dastuurka oo dowladdu meel-marsatay ayna dhaqan-gelinayso. Fiqi ayaa ku eedeeyay siyaasiyiinta mucaaradka ah inay Abu Dhabi kula kulmeen dhinacyo xiriir la leh RSF, isagoo sheegay in kulamadaasi ay la xiriiraan qorshayaal looga soo horjeedo dowladnimada Soomaaliya. Wasiirka ayaa sidoo kale ku eedeeyay mucaaradka in ay la soo noqon doonaan shirqoollo ka dhan ah dowladnimada iyo nabadda, ayna isku dayi doonaan inay maleeshiyaad uruuris iyo hoggaamiye-kooxeednimo bilaabaan, sida uu hadalka u dhigay. Dowladda Soomaaliya ayuu sheegay inay waajib ku tahay inay si adag uga hortagto cid walba oo halis gelinaysa nabadda iyo dowladnimada, qaranimada iyo madax-bannaanida dalka. “Khaa’inul-wadan kastaana abaalkiisa la marsiin doono,” ayuu Fiqi ku yiri qoraal uu dhawaan soo saaray. Si kastaba, arrimahan ayaa imanaya xilli xiisadda siyaasadeed ee dalka ay mareyso meel xasaasi ah, isla markaana ay mucaaradka iyo dowladda isku mari la’yihiin doorashooyinka iyo wax ka beddelka dastuurka oo dowladdu meel-marsatay ayna dhaqan-gelinayso. items.title: Eritrean troops seen in Ethiopia’s Tigray as fears of wider conflict grow
items.description: ADDIS ABABA (Somaliguardian) – Eritrean soldiers drove through the northern Ethiopian town of Adigrat on Wednesday, two witnesses told Reuters, days after the ​Horn of Africa neighbours severed diplomatic ties, raising fears of outright conflict. The sightings of Eritrean troops would be the first confirmation of ‌their presence on Ethiopian soil during the conflict in the country’s north, opens new tab between the federal government and a rebel alliance that broke out last month. Eritrea’s information minister Yemane Gebremeskel denied Eritrean forces were there, calling the witness accounts part of an Ethiopian plan to justify a war of aggression against its smaller neighbour. Ethiopia has accused Eritrea of ​backing the rebel alliance battling federal government troops since September 23 in the northern regions of Tigray, Amhara and Afar. Afar’s chief ​administrator said last week that Eritrean troops were fighting in his region, but Reuters could not confirm that. Asmara ⁠has denied the allegations, which led to the severing of diplomatic ties last week. Spokespeople for Ethiopia’s government and Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed did not ​immediately respond to requests for comment. WITNESSES SAW ERITREAN TROOPS DRIVING THROUGH TOWN Two residents of Adigrat, a town in Tigray about 25 km (15 miles) south ​of the Eritrean border that has not experienced clashes during the current conflict, said they had seen two trucks with dozens of Eritrean soldiers driving through the town on Wednesday morning. They said they could identify the soldiers as Eritrean by their off-white camouflage uniforms. Another Adigrat resident who was not in town at the time said family ​members had told him they had also seen Eritrean troops. Reuters could not independently verify their accounts. All spoke on condition of anonymity because of ​security concerns related to the ongoing conflict. The Eritrean information minister Yemane said the allegations were intended to provide Ethiopia with a pretext to attack Eritrea. For over ‌three years, ⁠Abiy and other Ethiopian officials have repeatedly said that sea access is vital for their landlocked country’s security and economy. Asmara views those comments as an implicit threat against it, while Addis Ababa has said it aims to gain sea access peacefully. Ethiopia “has tried to re-package this war agenda in terms of self-defence by fabricating various allegations against Eritrea,” Yemane said. “So we connect the dots.” NORTHERN ETHIOPIA CONFLICT FUELS FEARS OF WIDER WAR Eritrean soldiers fought in ​support of Ethiopia’s federal government during ​a 2020-2022 civil war in ⁠Tigray. Some of them remained in northern parts of Tigray close to the border well after the war ended, according to Ethiopia’s government, UN experts and human rights organisations. Eritrea denied this. The fighting that broke out last month ​has raised fear that unrest could spread beyond Ethiopia’s borders in an increasingly fragile region where other ​powers are competing for ⁠influence. Tigray has Ethiopia’s longtime foe Eritrea to its north, and Sudan — caught up in a more than three-year-old civil war — to its west. Ethiopia’s government has also accused Egypt and Sudan of supporting the opposition alliance. Both have denied this. On Saturday, the US State Department urged Asmara and Addis Ababa to exercise ⁠restraint, warning ​that a conflict would jeopardise US collaboration with both countries. Eritrea, a former province of ​Ethiopia, won its statehood in 1993 after a 30-year independence struggle. The two countries fought a border war from 1998-2000 that killed tens of thousands. They normalised diplomatic relations in 2018, ​winning Abiy the Nobel Peace Prize, but relations soured once again during the 2020-2022 Tigray war. Contact us: info@somaliguardian.com

items.title: Mas’uuliyiinta DF oo lagu amray inay baneeyaan xilka wasiirnimo ama xildhibaan
items.description: Muqdisho (Caasimada Online) – Soomaaliya ayaa 14 sano kadib u gudbaysa nidaam cusub oo mamnuucaya in hal mas’uul uu isku mar wada hayo xilalka wasiirka iyo xildhibaanka, kadib markii wax laga beddelay qodobkii Dastuurka ee arrintaas oggolaanayay. Qodobka 97-aad ee dastuurkii KMG ahaa ee 2012 ayaa oggolaanayay in xildhibaan uu kamid noqdo Golaha Wasiirrada, balse qodobkaasi hadda meesha ayaa laga saaray, iyadoo la dhaqan-gelinayo nidaam kala saaraya labada xil. Xafiiska Guddoomiyaha Guddiga Madaxbannaan ee Dib-u-eegista iyo Hirgelinta Dastuurka, Avv. Burhaan Aadan Cumar ayaa Golaha Wasiirrada u diray ogeysiis ku saabsan waajibaadka ka dhalanaya isbeddelkan dastuuriga ah. Sida lagu sheegay bayaanka, xubnaha Golaha Wasiirrada ee sidoo kale ah xildhibaanno ayaa loo sheegay inay kala doortaan labada xil, iyadoo muddada lixda bilood ah ee loo qabtay in qodobka cusub uu dhaqan-galo ay bilaabatay 14-kii April 2026, kuna eg tahay 14-ka October 2026. “Wasiirka xildhibaan ah wuxuu luminayaa xubinnimada Golaha Wasiirrada. Sidoo kale, xildhibaanku wuxuu luminayaa xildhibaannimada haddii uu aqbalo xil kale oo dawli ah,” ayaa lagu yiri bayaanka Guddoomiyaha Guddiga. Arrintan ayaa ka dhigan in mas’uulka haya xil wasiirnimo uusan sii wadan karin xubinnimada Golaha Shacabka haddii uu doonayo inuu sii hayo xilka dowladda, halka xildhibaanka aqbala xil kale oo dowladeed uu luminayo xubinnimadiisa baarlamaanka. Isbeddelkan ayaa sidoo kale lagu micneeyay tallaabo lagu kala saarayo awoodaha hay’adaha sharci-dejinta iyo fulinta, si labada dhinac ay u gutaan waajibaadkooda dastuuriga ah, oo ay ku jirto isla-xisaabtanka. Marka ay dhammaato muddada kala-guurka ah ee ku eg 14-ka October 2026, mas’uuliyiinta ay khusayso ayaa laga doonayaa inay doortaan mid kamid ah labada xil, taas oo soo afjareysa dhaqankii ahaa in hal qof uu isku mar ka tirsanaado Golaha Wasiirrada iyo Baarlamaanka. items.title: Xaalad amni-darro oo kasoo korortay Jowhar iyo taliska booliska oo…
items.description: Jowhar (Caasimada Online) – Taliska Booliska HirShabelle ayaa ku dhawaaqay tallaabooyin adag oo ka dhan ah kooxaha loo yaqaanno ciyaal weerada ee ku sugan magaalada Jowhar, iyadoo taliska uu sheegay in falalkooda ay gaareen heer amni-darro ku abuuray shacabka iyo dadka isticmaala gaadiidka. Sarreeye Guuto Xasan Dhicisow Xasan oo maanta shir jaraa’id ku qabtay saldhigga booliska Jowhar ayaa sheegay in kooxahan ay si weyn ugu bateen waddooyinka magaalada, isla markaana ay dhibaato ku hayaan shacabka, ciidamada iyo dadka isticmaala gaadiidka. “Shirka jaraa’id wuxuu ku saabsan yahay ciyaal weerada.Magaalada Jowhar waxaa ku soo batay ciyaal weero. Ciyaal weeradaas oo loo maara la’ yahay magaaladii,” ayuu yiri Taliyaha Booliska HirShabelle. Sida uu sheegay Taliyaha, kooxahan ayaa dhagxaan ku tuura dadka ay waddooyinka maraya, iyadoo uusan jirin kala-sooc u dhexeeya dadka waayeelka ah iyo carruurta. Waxa uu sidoo kale sheegay inay mararka qaar istaagaan waddooyinka, caqabadna ku noqdaan ciidamada iyo gaadiidka, isla markaana ay isku dayaan inay xoog lacago uga qaataan dadka iyo gaadiidka. Xasan Dhicisow ayaa sheegay in xaaladda kooxahan ay ka gudubtay magaca “ciyaal weero”, isla markaana ay hadda isu beddeleen waxa uu ku tilmaamay “ciyaal burcad”, taas oo uu sheegay inay muujinayso heerka ay gaareen falalka ay geysanayaan. Taliska Booliska HirShabelle ayaa sheegay inuu go’aan ka qaatay arrintan, isagoo xusay in ciidamada ammaanka la siiyay awood buuxda oo ay kula tacaalaan kooxahaas. “Cadawga Al-Shabaab sidaan ula dagaallanno, sidaas ayaa maanta laga bilaabo ula dagaallamaynaa ciyaal weero,” ayuu yiri taliyaha oo sheegay in dadka lagu helo falalkaasi ay wajihi doonaan tallaabooyin sharci ah oo ay kamid yihiin xarig iyo maxkamadeyn, isagoo sidoo kale sheegay in ciidamada ay qaadi doonaan tallaabooyin kale oo amni. Sidoo kale, Taliyaha booliska ayaa diray digniin uu ku sheegay inay tahay mid kama dambeys ah, taas oo waalidiinta carruurtooda lagu eedeeyo inay ku jiraan kooxahaas ku faray inay si degdeg ah gacanta ugu dhigaan oo ay ka joojiyaan falalka amni-darrada ah. “Waalidkii dhalay ilmahaas, ilmihiinna gacanta ka qabsada. Waxaan idin leeyahay ilmihiinna gacanta ka qabsada,” ayuu yiri Xasan Dhicisow oo ugu baaqay hooyooyinka iyo aabbayaasha inay carruurtooda gacanta ku hayaan, kana reebaan falalka uu sheegay inay khatar ku yihiin amniga magaalada Jowhar. Waxa uu intaas ku daray in ciidamada ammaanku ay garanayaan qaar kamid ah dhallinyarada uu sheegay inay ku dhuumaleysanayaan goobo ku yaalla magaalada Jowhar, isagoo waalidiinta uga digay inay carruurtooda u oggolaadaan inay sii wadaan falalka lagu eedeeyay. “Maanta kadibna waalidka iiguma iman karo ciyaalkaas. Kii far-dheer ka soo naqda annagaa tallaabo ka qaadeyna,” ayuu yiri Taliyaha, oo xitaa rabshadaha ciyaal-weerada gaaraiiyay inay xiriir la yeelan karto kooxda argagixisada Al-Shabaab. “Waxaan dareemeynaa in la soo adeegsaday. Al-Shabaab inay xiriir lala leedahay oo meeshaas laga soo adeegsadaan dareemeynaa ciyaal weerada,” ayuu hadalkiisa sii raaciyay. Wuxuu sheegay in qaar kamid ah falalka kooxahan lagu eedeeyay ay u muuqdaan kuwo la mid ah falal ay horey u sameyn jireen Al-Shabaab, inkastoo hadalkaas uu taliyaha ku saleeyay tuhun uu sheegay inuu jiro. items.title: Soomaaliya iyo Azerbaijan oo maanta yeeshay wada-hadalo cusub oo muhiim ah
items.description: Baku (Caasimada Online) – Safiirka Jamhuuriyadda Federaalka Soomaaliya ee dalka Azerbaijan, Danjire Cabdinuur Daahir Fiidoow ayaa kulan muhiim ah la qaatay Wasiirka Wasaaradda Sayniska iyo Waxbarashada ee Jamhuuriyadda Azerbaijan, Emin Amrullayev. Kulanka ayaa diiradda lagu saaray xoojinta iskaashiga waxbarasho ee Soomaaliya iyo Azerbaijan, gaar ahaan ballaarinta fursadaha waxbarasho ee ay heli karaan ardayda Soomaaliyeed. Labada dhinac ayaa sidoo kale ka wada-hadlay taageerada ardayda Soomaaliyeed ee wax ka barata Azerbaijan iyo sidii loo abuuri lahaa fursado dheeraad ah oo ay ka faa’iideystaan, gaar ahaan dhinacyada tacliinta sare iyo waxbarashada. Danjire Cabdinuur Fiidoow iyo Wasiir Emin Amrullayev ayaa sidoo kale isla eegay horumarinta xiriirka iyo iskaashiga u dhexeeya hay’adaha waxbarashada ee labada dal. Intii uu kulanku socday, waxaa xoogga la saaray dhiirrigelinta tacliinta sare iyo dhisidda iskaashi waara oo dhinaca waxbarashada ah, kaas oo fursado cusub u abuuri kara ardayda iyo hay’adaha waxbarashada ee labada dal. Danjire Cabdinuur Daahir Fiidoow ayaa uga mahadceliyey Wasiir Emin Amrullayev iyo Wasaaradda Sayniska iyo Waxbarashada Azerbaijan soo dhoweynta diirran iyo taageerada ay siiyaan ardayda Soomaaliyeed ee dalkaasi wax ka barata. Safiirka ayaa xusay muhiimadda ay waxbarashadu u leedahay xiriirka sii kobcaya ee Soomaaliya iyo Azerbaijan, isagoo sheegay in Safaaradda Soomaaliya ay mudnaan gaar ah siinayso ballaarinta fursadaha waxbarasho ee ay helaan ardayda Soomaaliyeed. Kulanka ayaa kusoo aadaya iyadoo labada dal ay wadaan dadaallo lagu xoojinayo xiriirkooda, iyadoo waxbarashada iyo tacliinta sare ay kamid yihiin dhinacyada muhiimka ah ee lagu horumarin karo iskaashiga Soomaaliya iyo Azerbaijan. items.title: Guddiga Madaxabannaan ee Dib-u-eegista iyo Hirgelinta Dastuurka oo xusuusisay Xukuumadda in 14-ka Oktoobar ay dhaqan-gelayaan qodobbada kala saaraya Xildhibaannada iyo Wasiirrada
items.description: Muqdisho, 7 Oktoobar 2026: Guddiga Madaxabannaan ee Dib-u-eegista iyo Hirgelinta Dastuurka (GMDHD) ayaa soo saaray warsaxaafadeed ku saabsan dhaqan-gelinta qaar ka mid ah qodobbada Dastuurka Jamhuuriyadda Federaalka Soomaaliya ee 2026. Guddoomiyaha Guddiga, Avv. Burhaan Aadan Cumar, ayaa sheegay in muddadii lixda bilood ahayd ee loo asteeyay in tallaabooyinka maamul lagu waafajiyo Dastuurka cusub ay ku egyahay 14-ka Oktoobar 2026. Guddigu wuxuu caddeeyay in laga bilaabo 14-ka Oktoobar ay dhaqan-gelayaan Qodobka 81aad, Faqraddiisa 1aad, xarafka (f), iyo Qodobka 117aad, Faqradda 3(a), kuwaas oo dhigaya kala saaridda xilalka xildhibaannimada iyo xubinnimada Golaha Wasiirrada. Sida uu Guddigu sheegay, marka qodobbadan ay dhaqan-galaan, xildhibaanka noqda wasiir uu luminayo xubinnimada Golaha Wasiirrada, halka xildhibaanka aqbala xil kale oo dowladeed uu luminayo xildhibaannimadiisa. GMDHD ayaa sidoo kale tilmaamay in hirgelinta qodobbadan ay tahay waajib dastuuri ah, iyadoo Qodobka 4aad ee Dastuurka uu dhigayo in Dastuurku yahay xeerka ugu sarreeya dalka, marka laga reebo Shareecada Islaamka, ayna waajib ku tahay dhammaan hay’adaha dowladda inay u hoggaansamaan. Warsaxaafadda Guddiga ayaa kusoo beegmaysa iyadoo ay wax ka yar toddobaad ka harsan tahay waqtiga loo asteeyay in qodobbadan ay si rasmi ah u dhaqan-galaan.

items.title: Marka Tensions Rise as Gorgor Deployment Fuels Fears of Political Confrontation
items.description: Replacing 14 October Forces With Gorgor Raises Fears That a Political Dispute Could Become a New Security Crisis in Lower Shabelle MARKA (WDN) — A new security confrontation is taking shape in Marka, where the deployment of Somali National Army Gorgor forces has triggered growing tension and raised fears that a political dispute over the emerging North-South State could turn into an armed confrontation. The central question is no longer simply why additional troops have arrived. It is why the 14 October Brigade was moved out, why Gorgor was brought in, and whether national military forces are being used to resolve a political dispute that should instead be addressed through dialogue. Local reporting says Gorgor forces have established positions in Marka after security responsibilities previously associated with the 14 October Brigade were transferred. The deployment has already generated opposition among some local communities and political actors. For supporters of the emerging North-South State, the arrival of Gorgor is being interpreted not as a routine counterterrorism deployment but as an attempt to prevent their political project from taking shape. That interpretation remains an allegation, not an established fact. But the perception itself is becoming a security concern. Why the 14 October Brigade Matters to Marka The 14 October Brigade has a different history in Lower Shabelle. The unit was established during former President Mohamed Abdullahi Mohamed Farmaajo’s administration and became involved in military operations against Al-Shabaab in the region. For many residents of Marka and surrounding communities, the brigade’s presence has therefore been associated with the fight against Al-Shabaab rather than with an internal political dispute. Government reporting has previously described the 14 October Brigade operating alongside Gorgor and NISA against Al-Shabaab in the Marka area. In January 2026, Somali government forces said their joint operation had pushed Al-Shabaab fighters out of the Jilib Marka area, with residents welcoming the national forces. That history helps explain why the removal of the 14 October Brigade is politically sensitive. For residents who credit the unit with fighting Al-Shabaab, replacing it with another federal formation raises a different question: what has changed in the mission? The North-South State Changes the Equation The deployment comes as sections of the local population in the Shabelle regions have begun advocating for a new political administration they call the North-South State. The movement has transformed Marka from simply a security front into a political flashpoint. Supporters say they are seeking a new political arrangement and greater local authority. Federal authorities, meanwhile, have not recognized the emerging administration as an established federal entity. That disagreement should ordinarily be resolved through political dialogue. Instead, the presence of heavily armed national forces has created fears among supporters of the new administration that military pressure could be used to prevent the political project from advancing. The danger is that a political disagreement could become a security confrontation before the political issues are even negotiated. The Most Dangerous Consequence The greatest risk is not simply another clash in Marka. It is what could happen afterward. If Gorgor forces are perceived by local communities as humiliating, attacking or killing people associated with the North-South State movement, the political balance could change dramatically. Communities that currently regard the Federal Government as a political opponent may begin to view it as a direct security threat. That could create incentives for local actors to seek alternative alliances, including arrangements with armed groups that the government is fighting. Somalia has already seen how quickly political alienation can undermine counterterrorism campaigns. Hiiraan provides an important warning. Local clan militias initially played a major role in pushing Al-Shabaab out of parts of the region. But EUAA reporting documented how political disputes, inter-clan tensions and inadequate support for local forces contributed to the weakening of the counteroffensive and allowed Al-Shabaab to regain territory. More recently, reports have emerged of an understanding between sections of the Hawadle community and Al-Shabaab after prolonged conflict, although the scope and significance of that understanding remain contested and should not be interpreted as representing the entire Hawadle community. The lesson is not that every political dispute produces an alliance with Al-Shabaab. The lesson is more basic: When communities lose confidence in the political and security system, Al-Shabaab can find opportunities that did not previously exist. The Army Should Not Become the Political Battlefield This is why the Marka deployment deserves close attention. The Somali National Army’s primary responsibility is to protect citizens and fight armed groups threatening the state. Using national forces in a political dispute risks blurring that mission. If the federal government believes the Gorgor deployment is necessary to protect Marka from Al-Shabaab, it should clearly explain the security threat and the military’s mandate. If the principal objective is instead to prevent the North-South State from organizing politically, then the government faces a fundamentally political problem that cannot be resolved through military deployment. Political movements are not defeated permanently by soldiers. They are resolved through negotiations, representation and legitimate political agreements. A Warning From Hiiraan The developments in Hiiraan make this moment even more sensitive. Hawadle elders and political leaders have recently demanded that the Hirshabelle political process in Hiiraan be suspended until an agreement is reached over representation and power-sharing. They have explicitly called for dialogue and community consultation. The situation demonstrates how political grievances can become intertwined with security questions. The danger for Lower Shabelle is that the same pattern could emerge there: a community begins with political demands, the government responds with security measures, confrontation deepens, and local actors begin searching for alternative ways to protect their interests. That is precisely the cycle Somalia should avoid. The Choice Before Mogadishu The government still has an opportunity to prevent the Marka dispute from becoming a wider security crisis. It can make the mission of the Gorgor forces transparent, guarantee the protection of civilians and political actors, and open direct dialogue with the communities supporting the North-South State initiative. Most importantly, it can avoid turning the national army into the mechanism through which a political disagreement is settled. Because the consequences could extend far beyond Marka. If local communities come to believe that the Federal Government is using national forces to suppress their political aspirations, the government may not simply lose political support. It could weaken the very local cooperation that is essential to keeping Al-Shabaab out of Lower Shabelle. The experience of Hiiraan demonstrates the danger of allowing political grievances and security operations to reinforce each other. For Marka, the warning is therefore clear: Do not turn a political disagreement into a military confrontation. The 14 October Brigade’s legacy in Lower Shabelle is tied to the fight against Al-Shabaab. The arrival of Gorgor should not create a new battlefield between the Somali state and the communities it is supposed to protect. Because if political pressure turns into humiliation, violence and bloodshed, the political table could be overturned—and the space created by that confrontation could be exploited by Al-Shabaab. items.title: Before We Blame Others, Somalia Must Learn to Judge Itself
items.description: By Abdikarim Buh There is an old Somali story about a man who confidently claimed that he would never lose a case before a traditional court. When people asked how he could be so certain, his answer was simple: before taking another person to court, he first put himself on trial. He would examine his own conduct and ask whether he was right or wrong. If his conscience told him that he was at fault, he would abandon the case rather than accuse another person unjustly. That simple story contains a profound lesson for Somalia today: Before pointing a finger at others, we must have the courage to look at ourselves. For decades, Somalis have debated the causes of political instability, institutional weakness, insecurity and economic hardship. We frequently identify foreign interference, neighbouring governments, international powers or rival political actors as the source of our problems. Sometimes those accusations are justified. External actors do pursue their own interests, and foreign decisions can have serious consequences for Somalia. But there is another question we ask far less often: What part of Somalia’s problems have we created ourselves? That is the question this generation must confront. The First Court Is Our Own Conscience The wisdom of the Somali story can be turned into a practical method for dealing with almost any dispute. Before blaming another person, government or institution, we should ask four questions: What actually happened? Facts must come before accusations. Rumours, assumptions and political emotions cannot substitute for evidence. What was my contribution to the problem? This is the most difficult question because it requires us to acknowledge our own mistakes. What was beyond my control? Self-examination does not mean accepting responsibility for everything. It means distinguishing between what we caused, what we influenced and what was imposed upon us. What must I change to prevent the problem from happening again? That final question transforms self-criticism into responsibility. These principles are not merely useful in private disputes. They apply equally to political leadership, public administration, education, business and national affairs. Somali society possesses an extraordinary tradition of wisdom expressed through proverbs, poetry, storytelling and customary law. Our ancestors developed mechanisms for resolving disputes, restoring relationships and reminding individuals of their obligations to the wider community. The tragedy is that we sometimes celebrate this heritage without applying its lessons. A society that possesses wisdom but refuses to practice it cannot expect wisdom to rescue it. The Politics of Blaming Foreigners Few habits have become more familiar in Somali political discourse than blaming outsiders. Whenever Somalia experiences a political crisis, there is often an immediate search for an external sponsor. One country is accused of supporting one faction. Another is blamed for interfering in elections. Foreign governments are accused of manipulating political leaders or pursuing hidden agendas. Some of these claims may be true. International politics is not driven by charity. Every government protects what it considers its national interests. Countries cooperate when their interests coincide and compete when they diverge.  Somalia should therefore approach foreign policy with realism rather than illusion. The responsibility of Somali leaders is not simply to complain when foreign governments pursue their own interests. It is to understand those interests, negotiate intelligently, protect Somalia’s priorities, strengthen national institutions and reduce the internal weaknesses that make external influence easier. This leads to a harder question. If foreign governments can influence Somalia so easily, what conditions inside Somalia make that influence possible? Are our institutions strong enough? Do our political leaders share even a basic understanding of the national interest? Are disagreements resolved through institutions and agreed rules? Do political agreements survive changes in leadership? Do we have a national strategy that is stronger than individual political ambitions? These questions are far more productive than endlessly asking who is interfering in Somalia. Recognizing foreign interference is realism. Refusing to examine our own weaknesses is self-deception. Somalia’s Political Crisis Is Also a Crisis of Accountability The country’s political disputes provide perhaps the clearest test of this principle. Somalia’s Provisional Federal Constitution, adopted in 2012 after years of political negotiations, established a framework for governance and relations between the federal government and federal member states. But a constitution cannot protect a country simply because it is written on paper. It must be respected by political leaders, implemented by institutions and interpreted through legitimate procedures. Where constitutional questions remain unresolved, the answer should be negotiation and lawful clarification—not selective interpretation based on political convenience. Somalia has repeatedly struggled with disputes over elections, political mandates, federal authority and constitutional interpretation. Political actors frequently accuse one another of violating agreements or undermining the national interest. Others blame foreign governments for creating or prolonging the deadlock. But every political crisis should begin with a more uncomfortable examination: Did we honour the agreements we signed? Did we respect the rules when those rules worked against our interests? Were we prepared to compromise? Did we consult those affected by our decisions? Did we put the country’s long-term interests ahead of short-term political advantage? These questions must apply to everyone. No political leader, party, federal institution or regional administration should be able to treat constitutional rules as binding only when they are convenient. Likewise, political agreements cannot be respected selectively. A country cannot build institutions if its political leaders regard rules as optional. Self-Criticism Is Not Self-Blame There is an important distinction between accepting responsibility and accepting blame for everything. Somalia has genuinely faced external interference, regional rivalries, security threats, economic pressures and historical injustices. Acknowledging those realities does not require us to deny our own failures. Indeed, the opposite is true. A mature nation should be capable of saying both: “Others have contributed to our problems.” And: “We must take responsibility for the choices we ourselves have made.” That is not weakness. It is political maturity. The strongest societies are not those that never make mistakes. They are those capable of recognizing mistakes, correcting them and learning from them. The Lesson Must Begin with the Next Generation Perhaps the most lasting solution lies in education. If Somalia wants a future generation capable of building accountable institutions, peaceful politics and a functioning state, children must learn more than examination skills and professional qualifications. They must also learn responsibility. A child should be taught to ask: What happened? What was my role? Did I act fairly? What could I have done differently? How can I correct my mistake? Such questions teach children that admitting an error is not humiliation.  It is a form of strength. They learn to distinguish criticism from personal attack, disagreement from hostility and accountability from punishment. Those habits, developed early, eventually become the foundations of responsible citizenship. The Somali Story Still Has Something to Teach Us The man in the old Somali story understood something that modern politics often forgets. Before demanding justice from others, we must first be willing to apply the same standard to ourselves. Somalia does not need leaders who are incapable of admitting mistakes. It does not need citizens who automatically believe every failure is somebody else’s fault. And it does not need a political culture in which every crisis begins with an accusation and ends without accountability. It needs something much harder: honesty before accusation, evidence before judgment, responsibility before blame and reconciliation before revenge. Our ancestors left us the wisdom. The challenge is whether we have the courage to practice it. Before Somalia asks who is responsible for its problems, perhaps the first question should be the one that old Somali wisdom has been asking for generations: “What is my responsibility?” Abdikarim H. Whenever Somalia experiences a political crisis, there is often an immediate search for an external sponsor. One country is accused of supporting one faction. Another is blamed for interfering in elections. Foreign governments are accused of manipulating political leaders or pursuing hidden agendas. Some of these claims may be true. International politics is not driven by charity. Every government protects what it considers its national interests. Countries cooperate when their interests coincide and compete when they diverge.  Somalia should therefore approach foreign policy with realism rather than illusion. The responsibility of Somali leaders is not simply to complain when foreign governments pursue their own interests. It is to understand those interests, negotiate intelligently, protect Somalia’s priorities, strengthen national institutions and reduce the internal weaknesses that make external influence easier. This leads to a harder question. If foreign governments can influence Somalia so easily, what conditions inside Somalia make that influence possible? Are our institutions strong enough? Do our political leaders share even a basic understanding of the national interest? Are disagreements resolved through institutions and agreed rules? Do political agreements survive changes in leadership? Do we have a national strategy that is stronger than individual political ambitions? These questions are far more productive than endlessly asking who is interfering in Somalia. Recognizing foreign interference is realism. Refusing to examine our own weaknesses is self-deception. Somalia’s Political Crisis Is Also a Crisis of Accountability The country’s political disputes provide perhaps the clearest test of this principle. Somalia’s Provisional Federal Constitution, adopted in 2012 after years of political negotiations, established a framework for governance and relations between the federal government and federal member states. But a constitution cannot protect a country simply because it is written on paper. It must be respected by political leaders, implemented by institutions and interpreted through legitimate procedures. Where constitutional questions remain unresolved, the answer should be negotiation and lawful clarification—not selective interpretation based on political convenience. Somalia has repeatedly struggled with disputes over elections, political mandates, federal authority and constitutional interpretation. Political actors frequently accuse one another of violating agreements or undermining the national interest. Others blame foreign governments for creating or prolonging the deadlock. But every political crisis should begin with a more uncomfortable examination: Did we honour the agreements we signed? Did we respect the rules when those rules worked against our interests? Were we prepared to compromise? Did we consult those affected by our decisions? Did we put the country’s long-term interests ahead of short-term political advantage? These questions must apply to everyone. No political leader, party, federal institution or regional administration should be able to treat constitutional rules as binding only when they are convenient. Likewise, political agreements cannot be respected selectively. A country cannot build institutions if its political leaders regard rules as optional. Self-Criticism Is Not Self-Blame There is an important distinction between accepting responsibility and accepting blame for everything. Somalia has genuinely faced external interference, regional rivalries, security threats, economic pressures and historical injustices. Acknowledging those realities does not require us to deny our own failures. Indeed, the opposite is true. A mature nation should be capable of saying both: “Others have contributed to our problems.” And: “We must take responsibility for the choices we ourselves have made.” That is not weakness. It is political maturity. The strongest societies are not those that never make mistakes. They are those capable of recognizing mistakes, correcting them and learning from them. The Lesson Must Begin with the Next Generation Perhaps the most lasting solution lies in education. If Somalia wants a future generation capable of building accountable institutions, peaceful politics and a functioning state, children must learn more than examination skills and professional qualifications. They must also learn responsibility. A child should be taught to ask: What happened? What was my role? Did I act fairly? What could I have done differently? How can I correct my mistake? Such questions teach children that admitting an error is not humiliation.  It is a form of strength. They learn to distinguish criticism from personal attack, disagreement from hostility and accountability from punishment. Those habits, developed early, eventually become the foundations of responsible citizenship. The Somali Story Still Has Something to Teach Us The man in the old Somali story understood something that modern politics often forgets. Before demanding justice from others, we must first be willing to apply the same standard to ourselves. Somalia does not need leaders who are incapable of admitting mistakes. It does not need citizens who automatically believe every failure is somebody else’s fault. And it does not need a political culture in which every crisis begins with an accusation and ends without accountability. It needs something much harder: honesty before accusation, evidence before judgment, responsibility before blame and reconciliation before revenge. Our ancestors left us the wisdom. The challenge is whether we have the courage to practice it. Before Somalia asks who is responsible for its problems, perhaps the first question should be the one that old Somali wisdom has been asking for generations: “What is my responsibility?” Abdikarim H. items.title: BF oo tallaabo ka qaadaya wasiirka caafimaadka kadib dhacdadii shalay + Video
items.description: Muqdisho (Caasimada Online) – Guddoomiye ku xigeenka Guddiga Warfaafinta Golaha Shacabka, Xildhibaan Maxamed Xasan Murjaan oo maanta la hadlay wariyeyaasha ayaa sheegay inay tallaabo ka qaadayaan Wasiirka Caafimaadka, Dr. Cali Xaaji, ayna wax ka waydiin doonaan dhacdadii shalay, kadib markii uu carooday isagoo horjoogo Guddiga Adeegga Bulshada ee Baaralamaanka oo su’aallo ka waydiinayay howlaha wasaaradda. Wasiirka ayaa Talaadadii diiday in Telefishinka Universal uu si toos ah u tabiyo su’aalaha ay xildhibaannadu weydiinayaan, isagoo dalbaday in la joojiyo baahinta tooska ah ee kulanka. Cali Xaaji ayaa shaaca ka qaaday in uusan ka jawaabi doonin su’aalaha xildhibaannada, haddii Telefishinka Universal uu sii wado baahinta tooska ah ee kulanka, isaga oo guddoomiyaha guddiga ka codsaday in wariyeyaasha Tv-gaas laga saaro hoolka. “Guddoomiye TV-ga Universal hoolka waa inay ka baxaan, haddii kale aniga su’aalaha kama jawaabayo. TV-ga wuu diidan yahay inuu joojiyo Live-ka, sidaas darteed haddii uusan baxaynin, annaga ayaa baxayna,” ayuu yiri Wasiir Cali Xaaji Aadan. Intaas kadib waxaa maanta soo jawaabay Xildhibaan Maxamed Xasan Murjaan oo ah guddoomiye ku xigeenka Guddiga Warfaafinta Golaha Shacabka, isaga oo sheegay inay u yeeri doonaan wasiirka, ayna tallaabo sharci ah ka qaadi doonaan, sida uu hadalka u dhigay. “Inuu wasiir soo fariisto oo uu dhoho Idaacad hebel ha’iga baxdo aad ayaan uga xunahay sharcigana ma qabo, hay’adahan waa madax bannaan yihiin waana ka xunahay, mana ka yeeli doono tallaabo sharci ah ayaan ka qaadeynaa wasiirka,” ayuu yiri Xildhibaan Murjaan. Sidoo kale wuxuu kusii daray “Warbaahinta madaxabannaan xaq ayay u leedahay wixii khaldan ayay sheegee, wixii saxana waa sheegee cid laga yeelaayana ma jirto”. Xildhibaanka ayaa sheegay in Sabtida soo socota ay u yeeri doonaan Wasiirka Caafimaadka Soomaaliya, ayna wax ka waydiin doonaan is hortaagga uu ku sameeyay Universal TV. “Wixii arrintaas ku kalifay Sabtiga ayuu sheegi doonaa, waxaana horkeeneynaa baarlamaanka, guddigana waa ku ballanay,” ayuu sii raaciyay xildhibaanku. items.title: Ciidamo Eriteriyaan ah oo lagu arkay Tigray, xiisadda Itoobiya oo isu beddelaysa khilaaf goboleed
items.description: Adigrat, Itoobiya — 7 Oktoobar 2026: Ciidamo ka tirsan Eriteriya ayaa maalmahan gudaha u galay gobolka Tigray ee waqooyiga Itoobiya, iyadoo ilo maxalli ah iyo dadka deegaanka ay sheegeen in ciidamo Eriteriyaan ah lagu arkay magaalada Adigrat, halka qaar kalena ay u dhaqaaqeen dhanka koonfureed ee magaalada Mekelle. Warbixintan waxaa soo werisay AFP, iyadoo xustay in xaaladdu ay sii kordhinayso walaaca laga qabo in dagaalka Tigray uu isu beddelo khilaaf ballaaran oo gobolka ah. Arrintan ayaa kusoo beegmaysa xilli ciidamada dowladda federaalka Itoobiya ay dib ula wareegeen Mekelle, caasimadda gobolka Tigray, kadib markii xoogagga TPLF ay ka baxeen magaalada. Ciidamada dowladda ayaa sidoo kale dib u qabsaday garoonka diyaaradaha ee Mekelle. Xiisadda ayaa horey uga dhex dhalatay Itoobiya iyo Eriteriya, iyadoo Addis Ababa ay Eriteriya ku eedeysay inay taageerayso isbahaysiga mucaaradka ee uu hoggaaminayo TPLF. Eriteriya ayaa beenisay eedeymahaas, halka labada dal ay 1-dii Oktoobar jareen xiriirkoodii diblomaasiyadeed. Dhanka kale, Masar, Eriteriya, Soomaaliya iyo Suudaan ayaa 4-tii Oktoobar ku yeeshay magaalada New Alamein ee dalka Masar shir afargeesood ah oo looga hadlay xaaladda Geeska Afrika iyo Badda Cas. Hoggaamiyeyaashu waxay ku heshiiyeen in la xoojiyo wada-tashiga iyo isku-duwidda arrimaha gobolka, iyadoo ay carrabka ku adkeeyeen ilaalinta madaxbannaanida iyo midnimada dalalka iyo in khilaafaadka lagu xalliyo hab nabadeed. Itoobiya ayaa tallaabooyinkan iyo isbahaysiyada gobolka ka dhex socda u aragta arrimo si toos ah u saameynaya ammaankeeda, iyadoo horey u sheegtay in Eriteriya, Masar iyo Suudaan ay taageerayaan xoogagga ka soo horjeeda dowladda Itoobiya. Dalalkaasi ayaa beeniyay taageero milatari oo ay siinayaan kooxaha mucaaradka. Xaaladda hadda ka taagan Tigray ayaa sidaas darteed dib u soo nooleysay cabsi laga qabo in colaaddii gudaha Itoobiya ay ku faafto dalalka deriska ah, gaar ahaan iyadoo xiriirka Itoobiya iyo Eriteriya uu si weyn u xumaaday. Midowga Afrika ayaa dhinacyada ugu baaqay is-xakameyn iyo in khilaafaadka lagu xalliyo wada-hadal.
